newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy considers house arrest for ex-SS captain.
newsitem.headline: Italy considers house arrest for ex-SS captain.

text.p: The Italian military prosecutor preparing a new war crimes trial of former SS captain Erich Priebke said on Thursday he was considering whether to recommend house arrest for the 83-year-old German.

Antonino Intelisano was responding to newspaper reports that Priebke, who has been in jail on remand for 11 months, would be moved to a Roman Catholic convent or monastery near Rome as early as Friday.
"We are studying the possibility...of agreeing to Priebke's release into house arrest but there is nothing concrete yet," Intelisano said.
Priebke, the oldest prisoner in Italy, faces re-trial after Italy's highest appeal court on Tuesday scrapped the contested August 1 verdict which capped his tumultuous first trial.

In that verdict, a military bench ruled 2-1 that Priebke was guilty of complicity in multiple murder for the 1944 SS massacre of 335 men and boys near Rome, but mitigating circumstances and an expired statute of limitations required that he be freed.
The massacre at the Ardeatine Caves south of Rome was Italy's worst World War Two atrocity.

Priebke never saw freedom. After being trapped for hours in the courthouse by protesters after the verdict, he was re-arrested when Germany indicated it wanted to extradite him for a war crimes trial there.
He has been detained since his extradition last November 21 from Argentina, where he had lived openly in the Andean ski resort of Bariloche for some 50 years.
Priebke was held in Rome's military prison before and during the trial and was transferred to one of Rome's civilian jails, Regina Coeli, after the verdict.
His lawyer, Velio di Rezze, said Priebke's release into house arrest, which the defence wants, was "still far away".
"We don't even know yet what authority has jurisdiction, civilian or military," he said. He told Reuters that Priebke was "at his lowest point physically and mentally".
Relatives of the massacre's victims, who were civil plaintiffs at Priebke's trial, have opposed previous moves to secure Priebke's release because they believe he would flee.
Di Rezze said on Wednesday he also would seek to move Priebke's second trial out of Rome on the grounds that he could not get a fair hearing.
No date has yet been set for the fresh trial although Intelisano has said he expects it to open in mid-December.

Priebke was assigned to the Gestapo's Rome headquarters when the SS ordered the massacre on March 24, 1944 in retaliation for a partisan bomb attack in Rome which killed 33 members of the German military.
The SS rounded up the victims from Gestapo headquarters, Regino Coeli jail and their homes and trucked them to the Ardeatine Caves where they were shot in groups of five.
Priebke admits shooting two people and checking names off a list but argues he had to follow orders or be killed himself.
